label: PART III
title: Changing Structure Safely
lead: Use small, named transformations that keep behavior stable and make the next change easier.

chapters.title: Composing methods
chapters.intro: These refactorings reshape code inside a function so each step has a clear name, scope, and level of abstraction.

concepts.title: Extract Method
concepts.definition: Extract Method moves a coherent block into a well-named method and replaces the original block with a call. Fowler's language-neutral modern name is Extract Function.
concepts.look_for: Extract a decision, calculation, or phase that deserves vocabulary, especially when it can be tested or changed independently.
concepts.python_expanded:
# Before: subtotal calculation was embedded in total().
def total(order):
    subtotal = 0
    for line in order.lines:
        subtotal += line.amount
    tax = tax_policy.calculate(subtotal, order.region)
    return subtotal + tax


# After: subtotal calculation has one named function.
def total(order):
    subtotal = calculate_subtotal(order.lines)
    tax = tax_policy.calculate(subtotal, order.region)
    return subtotal + tax


def calculate_subtotal(lines):
    subtotal = 0
    for line in lines:
        subtotal += line.amount
    return subtotal
concepts.walkthrough: The loop that accumulates line amounts moves from `Total` to `CalculateSubtotal`. `Total` now reads at one level of intent: calculate a subtotal, calculate tax, then combine them. `CalculateSubtotal` receives exactly the data its calculation needs and returns the same value the local variable previously held. No caller-observable result changes, which makes this a refactoring. The new name matters more than the reduced line count: it creates domain vocabulary and a focused test seam. Python performs the same movement into `calculate_subtotal`. If extraction requires passing a dozen intertwined locals, that friction may reveal a larger responsibility problem or motivate Replace Method with Method Object. Extracting `AddOne` from a single obvious expression would add navigation without meaning. Modern Fowler terminology says Extract Function because the move is not limited to object methods.
concepts.caution: Choose a name that states intent, not mechanics such as `ProcessData`. Do not extract trivial fragments unless the name or reuse genuinely improves comprehension.
concepts.related: Related: Long Method; Inline Method; Replace Method with Method Object

concepts.title: Inline Method
concepts.definition: Inline Method replaces a call with the called method's body when the method adds no useful name, hides an obvious expression, or obstructs a larger refactoring. Fowler also calls it Inline Function.
concepts.look_for: Inline a forwarding or trivial method when its name is no clearer than its implementation and no independent contract depends on it.
concepts.walkthrough: `IsEligible` merely restates `customer.Points >= 100` and has one caller. Replacing the call with that expression removes a jump without changing which customers receive `ApplyReward`. The refactoring is useful when a tiny wrapper obscures rather than clarifies or when inlining exposes a larger block that can be reorganized coherently. A one-line method is not automatically a candidate. `QualifiesForFreeShipping` may encode valuable domain vocabulary even if its body is short, and a port can preserve an architectural boundary with one method. The decision turns on whether the name, contract, override point, or dependency seam earns the indirection. Python's before and after versions make the same trade: fewer functions are not inherently better, but an unhelpful alias can be removed safely.
concepts.caution: Keep short methods that carry domain language, protect a boundary, support substitution, or isolate a volatile rule. Inline only when the indirection adds less meaning than cost.
concepts.related: Related: Extract Method; Lazy Class; Remove Middleman

concepts.title: Extract Variable
concepts.definition: Extract Variable assigns part of a dense expression to a well-named local so intermediate business meaning, units, or control decisions become visible.
concepts.look_for: Use it for non-obvious conditions, repeated subexpressions, debugging points, and values whose names explain why the final expression is true.
concepts.python_expanded:
# Before:
if customer.order_count >= 5 and customer.risk_score < 20:
    approve(customer)


# After:
has_enough_history = customer.order_count >= 5
has_low_risk = customer.risk_score < 20

if has_enough_history and has_low_risk:
    approve(customer)
concepts.walkthrough: The original conditional exposes two thresholds but not their meaning. `hasEnoughHistory` names why five orders matter, and `hasLowRisk` names what the risk comparison establishes. The final `if` now reads as the business decision while each local retains the exact Boolean value produced before. This is a behavior-preserving refactoring, not a new approval rule. The variables also provide useful breakpoints when investigating why a customer was rejected. Python uses the same names and ordinary evaluation. A local can become stale if underlying mutable state changes between assignment and use, so keep the extraction close to its consumer and preserve evaluation order when expressions have side effects. In simple arithmetic, too many names can interrupt a familiar formula; use them where meaning outweighs visual expansion.
concepts.caution: Do not name every subexpression. Keep simple mathematical flow intact, and avoid changing evaluation count or order when the original expression has side effects.
concepts.related: Related: Inline Temp; Extract Method; Introduce Explaining Variable

concepts.title: Inline Temp
concepts.definition: Inline Temp replaces a local variable with the expression that produced it when the variable adds no meaning or blocks another refactoring. The modern name is Inline Variable.
concepts.look_for: Inline a single-use alias whose name merely repeats the called query, provided evaluation remains safe and inexpensive.
concepts.python_expanded:
# Before:
base_price = order.calculate_base_price()
return base_price > 1_000


# After:
return order.calculate_base_price() > 1_000
concepts.walkthrough: `basePrice` is used once and says no more than `CalculateBasePrice`. Replacing it with the query produces the same comparison and removes an alias that readers must track. This small step can also prepare code for Extract Method or Replace Temp with Query by reducing local state. The safety condition matters: `CalculateBasePrice` must be evaluated the same number of times and at the same point relative to side effects. A temporary should remain when it captures a domain concept, documents units, avoids an expensive or nondeterministic repeat, or provides a valuable debugging point. Python has the same trade-off despite lighter declaration syntax. Inline Temp is not a character-count optimization; it removes a local only when the expression is already the clearest name for the value.
concepts.caution: Keep the local when it conveys domain meaning, freezes a snapshot, avoids repeated cost, or aids debugging. Preserve evaluation order and count.
concepts.related: Related: Extract Variable; Replace Temp with Query

concepts.title: Replace Temp with Query
concepts.definition: Replace Temp with Query moves a derived local calculation into a query method or function so several operations can request the value without depending on one method's temporary state.
concepts.look_for: Use it when the same derived value recurs, prevents method extraction, or belongs to an object's public vocabulary. Verify the query's cost and purity.
concepts.walkthrough: The subtotal calculation becomes `CalculateSubtotal`, a query that derives its result from `order.Lines`. `CalculateTotal` still evaluates it once, stores the meaningful result locally, and uses it for tax and final addition. Other operations can now ask the same query instead of copying the derivation or receiving a temporary from the original method. The behavior is preserved as long as the query uses the same inputs and has no side effects. This example deliberately avoids calling the query twice; a method name can hide substantial work, and recomputation would change the cost even if the numeric result matched. Python follows the same extraction into `calculate_subtotal`. In modern practice, this move is often described simply as extracting a pure function or exposing a derived query.
concepts.caution: Do not hide an expensive database call or repeated traversal behind an innocent property. Compute once, pass the value, or cache deliberately when cost matters.
concepts.related: Related: Extract Method; Inline Temp; Pure Function
concepts.modern_note: Often described today as extracting a pure function or derived query.

concepts.title: Split Temporary Variable
concepts.definition: Split Temporary Variable replaces one repeatedly assigned name with a separate variable for each distinct concept. Each name then keeps one meaning throughout its lifetime.
concepts.look_for: Split a local when it first represents one calculation and later another. Retain reassignment for genuine accumulation, iteration, or state progression.
concepts.python_expanded:
# Before:
result = 2 * (height + width)
print(result)
result = height * width
print(result)


# After:
perimeter = 2 * (height + width)
print(perimeter)

area = height * width
print(area)
concepts.walkthrough: In the before version, `result` first means perimeter and then area. A reader must track its current meaning by position, and later extraction or debugging is more error-prone. `perimeter` and `area` each represent one concept and are assigned once. The two printed numbers remain exactly the same and in the same order. This refactoring often reveals that the surrounding code contains distinct phases or calculations that can later become methods. Python benefits from the semantic names even though it does not declare local types. Reassignment is not inherently suspect: a running `total`, loop index, state-machine state, or retry count can represent one concept evolving over time. The signal is a name whose conceptual identity changes, not merely a value that changes.
concepts.caution: Do not split coherent accumulators or loop state into artificial names. The problem is changing what a variable represents, not ordinary mutation of one concept.
concepts.related: Related: Extract Variable; Remove Assignments to Parameters; Long Method

concepts.title: Remove Assignments to Parameters
concepts.definition: Remove Assignments to Parameters stops overwriting an input name with a normalized or transformed value. A new local preserves the parameter's original meaning throughout the method.
concepts.look_for: Apply it when a parameter begins as caller input and later silently means sanitized, clamped, parsed, or discounted data.
concepts.python_expanded:
# Before: price was overwritten with the clamped value.
def apply_discount(price):
    non_negative_price = max(0, price)
    discounted_price = non_negative_price * 0.90
    return discounted_price
concepts.walkthrough: `price` remains the caller-supplied input. `nonNegativePrice` names the normalized value, and `discountedPrice` names the final calculation. A debugger can now show all three meanings simultaneously, and later code cannot accidentally treat the clamped value as the original input. The returned amount is unchanged from the parameter-reassigning implementation. In C#, parameter reassignment does not normally change the caller's variable because arguments are passed by value unless explicitly marked, but it still changes what the local name means. Python rebinding likewise does not mutate the caller's scalar; the readability issue remains. Mutation of an object received as a parameter is a separate and often more consequential design question. Use a new name when the concept changes, not simply because a style rule bans all reassignment.
concepts.caution: Some code uses parameter rebinding idiomatically, but a distinct local is clearer whenever normalization or transformation changes the concept represented by the name.
concepts.related: Related: Split Temporary Variable; Extract Variable; Immutability

concepts.title: Replace Method with Method Object
concepts.definition: Replace Method with Method Object turns a complicated method into a short-lived object whose fields hold its working state. Fowler's broader modern name is Replace Function with Command.
concepts.look_for: Use it when interdependent locals make ordinary extraction awkward and the calculation has enough phases or testable decisions to justify an object.
concepts.walkthrough: A large pricing method may have locals that several phases share, making extraction require long parameter lists and tuple returns. `PriceCalculation` promotes `order`, `subtotal`, and `discount` to fields of one short-lived command. `Run` names the sequence, while `CalculateSubtotal` and `CalculateDiscount` can be edited and tested as focused phases. Creating the object and calling `Run` should produce the same price as the original method. The object is a technique for organizing a complicated calculation, not a new long-lived domain entity. Python uses the same temporary owner. First try simpler moves: extract pure functions, introduce a result value, or pass a few explicit parameters. A class adds lifecycle and state that every reader must understand, so it earns its place only when it unlocks clearer decomposition.
concepts.caution: Do not convert every multi-step function into a class. Prefer pure extracted functions and explicit result values until shared working state genuinely blocks them.
concepts.related: Related: Long Method; Extract Method; Command
concepts.modern_note: Modern name: Replace Function with Command.

concepts.title: Substitute Algorithm
concepts.definition: Substitute Algorithm replaces one implementation with a clearer, safer, faster, or more suitable algorithm while preserving the operation's stated contract.
concepts.look_for: Specify behavior for ordering, duplicates, casing, nulls, overflow, and edge cases; lock it with tests, then replace the implementation deliberately.
concepts.walkthrough: `UniqueSorted` promises a case-insensitive set of names in case-insensitive order. The replacement uses library collection algorithms instead of hand-written nested comparisons, while keeping the contract explicit through `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` in C# and `casefold` keys in Python. Tests should settle ambiguous details such as which spelling survives when both `Alice` and `ALICE` appear. An algorithm substitution can improve clarity or complexity, but equivalent-looking code often differs at edges: sort stability, culture sensitivity, duplicate retention, integer overflow, and exception behavior all matter. The code shown is the after implementation; the comment records what it replaced because reproducing a long inferior algorithm would obscure the concept. Use benchmarks when performance is the motivation and behavioral tests when correctness is the safety condition.
concepts.caution: Do not assume library calls are behaviorally identical to the old algorithm. Define edge semantics first and benchmark with representative data when performance motivates the change.
concepts.related: Related: Behavior-preserving change; Performance engineering; Property-based testing

chapters.title: Moving features between objects
chapters.intro: These refactorings move behavior and data toward the component that has the knowledge or responsibility to own them.

concepts.title: Move Method
concepts.definition: Move Method relocates behavior to the class or module whose data it uses most or whose responsibility it expresses. Fowler's language-neutral name is Move Function.
concepts.look_for: When a method mostly reads another object and makes a decision about that object, move it there; keep a forwarding wrapper temporarily if callers need migration time.
concepts.walkthrough: The discount method formerly lived in `PricingService` but depended primarily on `Customer.LifetimeSpend`. Moving it to `Customer.GetDiscountRate` places the threshold beside the value it interprets and lets callers ask the customer a domain question. The result remains the same: lifetime spend of at least 1,000 yields 10 percent. This is also a response to Feature Envy. The correct destination is not chosen by mechanically counting field accesses; business ownership matters. If discount rates are a campaign policy that changes independently of customers, an injected `DiscountPolicy` may be more honest. Python's method move follows the same reasoning. During a public API migration, the old service method can delegate to the customer temporarily, then be removed after callers move.
concepts.caution: A method coordinating several peers or expressing independent policy may belong in a service even if it reads one object heavily. Move behavior according to ownership, not a tally alone.
concepts.related: Related: Feature Envy; Move Field; Extract Class

concepts.title: Move Field
concepts.definition: Move Field relocates stored data to the class or module that owns its rules and uses it most. Data and the behavior governing it should share an intentional owner.
concepts.look_for: Move a field when nearly all reads and writes occur in behavior already belonging elsewhere, and when the destination controls its invariant and lifecycle.
concepts.walkthrough: `rate` belongs with `TaxPolicy` because that class validates and applies it. Leaving the field on `Order` would make orders carry policy configuration and force `TaxPolicy` to reach into another object's state. After the move, `Order` supplies only its `Subtotal`, while the policy owns both the rate and its rule. The calculated tax is unchanged. Field movement often follows Move Method: once behavior moves, the data used almost exclusively by that behavior becomes an obvious companion. Persistence and serialization make this refactoring less local than it appears. If `taxRate` was stored in an order table or public payload, a migration may need dual reads, backfill, versioned contracts, and compatibility checks. Python's runtime object model does not remove those external ownership concerns.
concepts.caution: Moving stored data can affect database schemas, serialization, caching, and ownership semantics. Plan external contract migration rather than treating it as a private rename.
concepts.related: Related: Move Method; Extract Class; Data ownership

concepts.title: Extract Class
concepts.definition: Extract Class creates a new class for a coherent subset of fields and behavior that already forms its own concept or reason to change.
concepts.look_for: Identify member clusters readers naturally describe with a noun. Move the data and the behavior that protects it together, then let the original class collaborate with the new type.
concepts.walkthrough: `CountryCode`, `Number`, and international formatting form a concept independent of a customer's name. `PhoneNumber` collects those values and owns the format operation; `Customer` now has a phone instead of knowing how a phone is assembled. Validation and normalization have an obvious future home, and other domain types can use phone numbers without copying fields. The goal is not merely to shorten `Customer`; the extracted class must be cohesive and independently meaningful. Python uses an ordinary class here so the explicit constructor and behavior remain visible. An immutable record or frozen dataclass could be a concise modern representation once the concept is understood. If the extracted object only mirrors a random subset of fields with no behavior, vocabulary, or separate change pressure, the refactoring has added navigation rather than design.
concepts.caution: An extracted class should own a real concept, invariant, or change boundary. Do not create a new type solely to reduce the original file's line count.
concepts.related: Related: Large Class; Data Clumps; Value Object

concepts.title: Inline Class
concepts.definition: Inline Class moves a class's data and behavior into another class when the separate abstraction no longer has independent meaning or responsibility.
concepts.look_for: Use it when a type only forwards calls or wraps a trivial value without validation, identity, units, or its own reason to change.
concepts.walkthrough: The former `CustomerName` class contributed nothing beyond storing a string and returning it through `Value`. Moving that field into `Customer.Name` removes an object and navigation step while preserving the displayed label. This is the inverse of Extract Class and often follows a design change that drained an old abstraction of responsibility. The decision hinges on meaning, not size. If `CustomerName` normalized whitespace, enforced length, handled localization, or prevented confusion with another string, it would remain a useful value object even with very little code. Python's direct `name` attribute represents the deliberately simple case. Public serialization and API schemas may still require migration if the wrapper's shape was externally visible.
concepts.caution: Keep a small value object when it prevents invalid states, distinguishes primitives, carries units, or owns formatting. Inline only an abstraction that truly adds no current meaning.
concepts.related: Related: Extract Class; Lazy Class; Inline Method

concepts.title: Hide Delegate
concepts.definition: Hide Delegate lets a client ask its direct collaborator for a meaningful operation instead of navigating through that collaborator to another object. Volatile object-graph knowledge stays with its owner.
concepts.look_for: Hide repeated or unstable chains when callers should know the requested action but not which nested collaborator performs it.
concepts.walkthrough: The original client knows two internal links: an order exposes its customer, and the customer exposes a notifications collaborator. `Order.NotifyCustomerAsync` replaces that navigation with the business action the caller intends. If Customer later changes notification providers or moves the capability, order clients remain stable. The method deliberately names `NotifyCustomer`, not the mechanical chain it hides. Python's version uses `_customer` to mark the relationship internal by convention and exposes the same action. Hide Delegate is the usual response to a Message Chain. Applied indiscriminately, however, it creates a Middleman with dozens of forwarding methods. Use it where the relationship is volatile, repeated, or outside the client's responsibility. A simple property traversal over stable immutable data may remain more transparent.
concepts.caution: Do not forward every collaborator method. Hide navigation that callers should not own; otherwise the receiving class can become a Middleman with an inflated interface.
concepts.related: Related: Message Chains; Law of Demeter; Middleman

concepts.title: Remove Middleman
concepts.definition: Remove forwarding methods when a class merely relays calls and no longer protects a useful boundary or policy.
concepts.look_for: A class has many one-line methods that expose another object's API without adding validation, translation, authorization, or coordination.
concepts.walkthrough: Before the refactoring, `Order.SendShippingNotice` and `Order.send_shipping_notice` do nothing except navigate to the customer's notification service and repeat the same call. The forwarding method suggests that `Order` owns a rule, but no order-specific rule exists. After removal, the client reaches `Customer.Notifications` directly, making the actual dependency visible and shrinking `Order`'s API. The behavior stays the same: the same notification component sends the same shipping notice. What changes is who knows about that component. This move is appropriate only because the example states that the client legitimately owns the relationship. If `Order` were enforcing permissions, selecting a template, recording an audit event, or shielding clients from a volatile vendor API, it would be a Facade or protective boundary rather than a useless middleman. Remove Middleman is therefore the inverse pressure of Hide Delegate: choose the side that leaves knowledge and policy in the most honest place.
concepts.caution: A small forwarding surface can preserve encapsulation or provide a migration seam. Remove it only after confirming that callers may safely depend on the underlying collaborator.
concepts.related: The inverse refactoring is Hide Delegate. Compare Facade, which intentionally offers a simpler or safer boundary rather than mechanically forwarding every operation.

concepts.title: Introduce Foreign Method
concepts.definition: Add one application-owned helper for an operation that conceptually belongs on a library or third-party type you cannot modify.
concepts.look_for: The same small calculation sits beside uses of an external type, but changing that type is impossible and a wrapper would be excessive.
concepts.python_expanded:
from datetime import timedelta


def next_business_day(value):
    candidate = value + timedelta(days=1)

    while candidate.weekday() >= 5:
        candidate = candidate + timedelta(days=1)

    return candidate


ship_date = next_business_day(order.paid_on)
concepts.walkthrough: `DateOnly` and Python's date type cannot be changed to include the application's idea of a business day. `NextBusinessDay` and `next_business_day` place that missing operation in application-owned code and give it domain vocabulary. The helper advances at least one day, skips Saturday and Sunday, and returns another value of the foreign type. Calling code no longer repeats that calculation. This is deliberately a single operation; it does not justify a complete date abstraction. The C# shorthand shows an extension method, which changes call-site syntax but does not actually add an instance member to `DateOnly`. Python has no direct extension-method equivalent, so a named module-level function remains straightforward. If holiday calendars, market-specific weekends, and cutoff times join this rule, the pressure changes: those related policies deserve a `BusinessCalendar` adapter or local extension object with dependencies, rather than an expanding pile of supposedly simple foreign methods.
concepts.caution: Keep the helper narrow. Several related operations or rules that need configuration indicate a local extension, adapter, or domain service instead.
concepts.related: Introduce Local Extension handles a cluster of missing operations. An extension method is C# syntax for the helper, not a different ownership model.

concepts.title: Introduce Local Extension
concepts.definition: Wrap an unmodifiable type in an application-owned type that collects several related domain operations.
concepts.look_for: Helpers around the same library type are multiplying, travel together, or need shared policy such as a holiday calendar.
concepts.walkthrough: `BusinessDate` wraps the unmodifiable date value and gathers two related application operations: `IsWorkingDay`/`is_working_day` and `NextWorkingDay`/`next_working_day`. It also carries the `IHolidayCalendar` dependency needed to answer those questions correctly. That shared dependency is the point at which scattered foreign methods would start becoming awkward. Callers now talk in shipping or scheduling vocabulary instead of reconstructing weekend and holiday rules around raw dates. The wrapper delegates ordinary date storage to `DateOnly` or Python's date object; it does not attempt to reproduce the whole foreign API. This is a local extension because the application owns the richer view of an external type. It also resembles a value object, but the labels answer different questions: Local Extension describes why the wrapper exists, while Value Object describes identity and equality semantics. Those semantics would need to be defined explicitly before using `BusinessDate` as a dictionary key or comparing instances.
concepts.caution: Translate only the application-specific surface. A wrapper that mirrors the entire library API creates maintenance work without clarifying the domain.
concepts.related: Introduce Foreign Method is lighter for one isolated operation. Adapter is closer when the purpose is translating between two existing contracts.

chapters.title: Organizing data
chapters.intro: These refactorings make ownership, identity, mutability, associations, and domain meaning explicit.

concepts.title: Self-Encapsulate Field
concepts.definition: Make a class use its own property or access methods instead of touching a field directly, creating one interception point inside the class.
concepts.look_for: Many methods read or write the same field directly, and validation, lazy loading, notifications, or a representation change is approaching.
concepts.walkthrough: `Thermostat` still stores the temperature in `_targetCelsius` or `_target_celsius`, but `IncreaseTarget` no longer edits that storage directly. It reads and writes through `TargetCelsius` or `target_celsius`, so the range check applies to changes made from inside the class as well as during construction. The observable result of a valid increase is unchanged. The new interception point makes a future unit conversion, notification, or lazy read local to the accessor instead of requiring edits in every method that touched the field. This refactoring is called self-encapsulation because the class is encapsulating the field from its own implementation, not merely from outside callers. C# properties and Python descriptors make the syntax look like field access, but method logic still runs. That can be useful, yet it also means a deceptively cheap-looking access can become expensive or surprising; keep accessor behavior predictable.
concepts.caution: Do not add ceremonial accessors to every private field. Use the seam when the field has evolving rules or representation, and keep property access unsurprising.
concepts.related: Encapsulate Field protects a public boundary; Self-Encapsulate Field changes how the owning class accesses its own storage.

concepts.title: Replace Data Value with Object
concepts.definition: Replace a primitive value with a domain object that owns its validation, normalization, formatting, units, or behavior.
concepts.look_for: The same string, number, or date is validated and manipulated in several places, or values with different meanings share the same primitive type.
concepts.walkthrough: Before the change, `RegisterCustomer`/`register_customer` accepts a plain string, so every consumer must remember how to validate and normalize an address. Afterward, the `EmailAddress` constructor rejects missing or malformed input, normalizes the stored `Value`, and provides `Domain`/`domain` where the related operation naturally belongs. The registration method can now require an `EmailAddress`, making an invalid raw string impossible to pass accidentally in C# and a clear contract violation in Python. The business operation has not changed; the representation and ownership of email rules have. This is the common move behind value objects, domain primitives, and the advice to avoid primitive obsession. A production email validator would be more careful than the teaching check shown here, but the design point remains: one concept has one place for its invariants. If equality should be based on the normalized address, the class should also implement value equality explicitly.
concepts.caution: The new type should eliminate invalid states or centralize real behavior. A wrapper with no invariants, operations, or type-safety benefit only adds friction.
concepts.related: This often produces a Value Object and addresses Primitive Obsession. Replace Type Code with Class is the same move applied specifically to categorical codes.

concepts.title: Change Value to Reference
concepts.definition: Replace interchangeable copies with one canonical object when the domain concept has identity and shared updates must be observed everywhere.
concepts.look_for: Several instances carry the same entity identifier, but changing one instance leaves the others stale or contradictory.
concepts.walkthrough: `CustomerRegistry.GetOrAdd` and `get_or_add` turn a customer identifier into a canonical `Customer` instance. Both orders receive the same object, even though the second lookup repeats the identifier. If the customer's name or account state changes through that object, both orders observe the change because they share a reference. Before this refactoring, code commonly reconstructed a new `Customer` value for each order; matching fields made the copies look equal, but updates could diverge. The registry now owns identity resolution and instance lifetime. That is the defining difference between an entity and a value: customer `customerId` persists while mutable attributes can change. In an ORM, identity maps and unit-of-work scopes often provide this behavior. A process-wide registry is not implied; the correct canonical scope might be one request, transaction, or session. Choosing too broad a scope creates stale caches and concurrency pressure.
concepts.caution: Canonical references introduce lifecycle, cache invalidation, and concurrency concerns. Define the identity key and the scope in which one instance is authoritative.
concepts.related: The inverse is Change Reference to Value. Identity Map is a common persistence implementation of the canonical-reference rule.

concepts.title: Change Reference to Value
concepts.definition: Replace identity-based mutable objects with immutable values when instances with the same contents should be interchangeable.
concepts.look_for: Objects have no independent lifecycle, are copied safely, and callers care about their contents rather than which instance they received.
concepts.walkthrough: `Coordinates` has no database identity or lifecycle separate from its latitude and longitude. The expanded implementations therefore expose no setters and define equality and hashing from those two components. Two independently constructed coordinates with the same contents compare as the same value and can safely serve as dictionary keys. That replaces reference identity with value semantics. The C# `readonly record struct` and Python frozen dataclass shorthand generate much of this ceremony, but the expanded versions show exactly what is being promised: immutability, component-wise equality, and a hash consistent with equality. This refactoring is appropriate for money, ranges, addresses, measurements, and similar concepts whose copies should not drift. It would be wrong for two customers who happen to share a name and address, because each customer retains independent identity and history. Value semantics also require every component to be immutable, or hashing and equality can become unstable after insertion into a set or dictionary.
concepts.caution: Do not convert an entity when independent identity, history, or lifecycle matters. Every field participating in equality must also have stable value semantics.
concepts.related: The inverse is Change Value to Reference. Records and frozen dataclasses are language mechanisms that make Value Object semantics concise.

concepts.title: Replace Array with Object
concepts.definition: Replace fixed positional slots with named fields when each position represents a different concept, unit, or rule.
concepts.look_for: Readers must remember that index 0 means one thing and index 1 another, or casts and bounds assumptions surround a supposedly simple array or tuple.
concepts.python_expanded:
# Before
raw_sample = ["api-01", 187, True]
host_name = raw_sample[0]
latency_milliseconds = raw_sample[1]


# After
class PerformanceSample:
    def __init__(self, host_name, latency_milliseconds, succeeded):
        self.host_name = host_name
        self.latency_milliseconds = latency_milliseconds
        self.succeeded = succeeded


sample = PerformanceSample("api-01", 187, True)
latency = sample.latency_milliseconds
concepts.walkthrough: The `rawSample`/`raw_sample` array has a hidden schema: host name at position 0, latency at position 1, and success at position 2. Nothing at an access site explains those meanings, and C# additionally needs casts from `object`. `PerformanceSample` gives each slot a stable name and type, so `sample.LatencyMilliseconds` documents both meaning and unit. The data represented by the example stays the same; only its representation changes. Once the object exists, validation such as non-negative latency or operations such as classifying slow samples have an obvious home. This refactoring applies to heterogeneous records encoded as arrays or tuples, not to genuinely homogeneous sequences such as a list of latencies. A lightweight record, named tuple, TypedDict, or dataclass may be enough in modern languages. The essential move is replacing positional knowledge with a named schema, not choosing the heaviest possible class.
concepts.caution: Keep homogeneous collections as collections. Introduce an object only when positions carry distinct meanings or invariants.
concepts.related: Related to Data Clumps and Introduce Parameter Object. Modern records, named tuples, and dataclasses are lighter implementation options.

concepts.title: Duplicate Observed Data
concepts.definition: Move domain data out of UI controls while maintaining an explicit synchronization path between the model and its displayed copy.
concepts.look_for: Business rules read directly from widgets, or a domain object contains control-specific state because the screen became the accidental source of truth.
concepts.walkthrough: The text displayed by `ICustomerView` is necessarily a second copy of `Customer.DisplayName`, but it is no longer the business record. `CustomerPresenter.Load` copies model state into the view. `DisplayNameEdited` sends user input back through `Customer.Rename` and then refreshes the view from the model's accepted value. That direction matters: `Customer` remains the source of truth, while the control contains a projection suitable for editing. The original Fowler refactoring predates today's binding frameworks, but the same problem appears in MVVM, React state, and web forms whenever UI state and domain state drift. A binding engine can automate notifications; it cannot decide ownership. This example makes synchronization explicit so validation and normalization stay in `Customer` rather than leaking into a text box. In a real editor, cancellation, validation messages, and unsaved drafts may justify a view-model copy with a deliberate commit operation rather than immediate two-way synchronization.
concepts.caution: Duplicated state can drift. Name the authoritative copy, synchronization direction, validation boundary, and commit timing explicitly.
concepts.related: Modern MVVM data binding and unidirectional UI state are descendants of this concern; they automate propagation but do not remove the ownership decision.
concepts.modern_note: The historical name sounds like duplication is the goal. The real goal is separating domain state from presentation state while controlling the unavoidable copy.

concepts.title: Change Unidirectional Association to Bidirectional
concepts.definition: Add reverse navigation when both objects genuinely need the relationship, and centralize updates so both ends remain consistent.
concepts.look_for: Code repeatedly searches from the target back to the source, and reverse navigation is a frequent domain operation rather than an occasional report query.
concepts.walkthrough: Originally an `Order` might know its customer while `Customer` had no route back to its orders. `Customer.AddOrder`/`add_order` now establishes both links as one operation: it inserts the order into `_orders` and calls `AssignCustomer`/`_assign_customer` to set the reverse reference. Callers cannot legitimately update just one side because the association-management method owns the invariant. `Customer.Orders` exposes a read-only view or tuple so external code cannot bypass that method. The result is bidirectional navigation: order to customer and customer to orders. This can simplify frequent domain operations such as calculating a customer's current open orders, but it creates synchronization, persistence, and serialization work. For an occasional reporting query, `OrderRepository.FindByCustomerId` would preserve a unidirectional object model and may be cleaner. Bidirectionality should model a real navigational need, not merely save one query.
concepts.caution: Every add, remove, reassign, load, and deserialize path must preserve both ends. Prefer a query when reverse navigation is rare.
concepts.related: The inverse is Change Bidirectional Association to Unidirectional. Encapsulate Collection helps prevent callers from corrupting one end.

concepts.title: Change Bidirectional Association to Unidirectional
concepts.definition: Remove an unnecessary back-reference and recover reverse navigation through a query when needed.
concepts.look_for: One navigation direction is unused, causes serialization cycles, or forces two objects to coordinate every relationship change.
concepts.walkthrough: After the refactoring, `Order` keeps the ownership-relevant direction through `CustomerId`; `Customer` no longer maintains a mutable `Orders` collection. When a use case needs reverse navigation, `OrderRepository.FindByCustomer`/`find_by_customer` derives it from the authoritative order records. Removing the back-reference eliminates the possibility that an order points at a customer while that customer's in-memory collection omits the order. It can also remove object-graph cycles that complicate serialization and persistence. The functional capability remains: clients can still obtain a customer's orders, but they ask a repository instead of traversing a stored association. The trade-off is query cost. A real repository should use an indexed database query rather than scan all orders as the teaching fragment does. Keep the direction that matches aggregate ownership and common mutations; provide a query model for less frequent reverse views.
concepts.caution: Replacing a reference with a query changes the cost model. Index important access paths and avoid repeated queries inside loops.
concepts.related: The inverse is Change Unidirectional Association to Bidirectional. This move often aligns with aggregate boundaries and CQRS read models.

concepts.title: Replace Magic Number with Symbolic Constant
concepts.definition: Give an unexplained literal a name that states its meaning, unit, and owner.
concepts.look_for: The same literal appears in a rule or calculation and a reader cannot tell whether it is a rate, limit, timeout, unit conversion, or coincidence.
concepts.python_expanded:
# Before
total = subtotal + (subtotal * 0.0825)

# After
LOCAL_SALES_TAX_RATE = 0.0825


def add_local_sales_tax(subtotal):
    tax = subtotal * LOCAL_SALES_TAX_RATE
    return subtotal + tax
concepts.walkthrough: `0.0825` gives no clue whether it is a tax, fee, probability, or tuning parameter. `LocalSalesTaxRate`/`LOCAL_SALES_TAX_RATE` names both the business meaning and the fact that the value is a rate. `AddLocalSalesTax` then shows where the constant participates in the calculation. Replacing the literal does not change the numerical result; it removes duplicated knowledge and gives future readers a searchable term. Ownership matters as much as naming. A conversion factor belongs near measurement code, while a checkout rule belongs with checkout policy. The example uses a constant only to illustrate the refactoring. Real sales-tax rates vary by jurisdiction and effective date, so freezing one in source code would likely be the wrong domain model. A symbolic name makes a stable literal understandable; it does not magically turn changing business data into a constant.
concepts.caution: Do not confuse a named constant with configurable policy. Values that vary by tenant, region, or time need data and effective-date rules.
concepts.related: Related to Primitive Obsession. Configuration replaces hard coding only when the value truly varies operationally.

concepts.title: Encapsulate Field
concepts.definition: Stop exposing mutable storage directly and route changes through a property or domain operation that protects invariants.
concepts.look_for: External callers can assign a field freely, bypass validation, or depend on its current representation.
concepts.walkthrough: The public field in the before form allows any caller to assign any balance, including values produced without a legitimate transaction. `BankAccount` now keeps `_balance` private, exposes `Balance`/`balance` as a read-only observation, and changes the value only through `Deposit`/`deposit`. That method names the business event and rejects non-positive amounts before modifying state. Existing read behavior remains available, while mutation gains one controlled path. This is stronger than mechanically replacing a field with public get and set accessors; a public setter would preserve the same unrestricted mutation under different syntax. Encapsulation creates room to add transaction recording, currency checks, or notifications without changing every caller. Plain immutable data does not need defensive getter ceremony, but mutable state with invariants benefits from behavior-oriented methods.
concepts.caution: A public setter may only disguise the original field. Prefer intention-revealing operations when mutations carry rules or side effects.
concepts.related: Self-Encapsulate Field concerns access from inside the class. Remove Setting Method narrows a property further to construction-only state.

concepts.title: Encapsulate Collection
concepts.definition: Keep a mutable collection private and expose observations plus operations that preserve the owner's rules.
concepts.look_for: Callers receive a list and can add, remove, reorder, or clear elements without validation, notifications, or reciprocal updates.
concepts.walkthrough: `PurchaseOrder` owns `_lines`; callers can observe a snapshot through `Lines` or an immutable tuple through `lines`, but they cannot append directly. `AddLine`/`add_line` is the single mutation path and enforces the positive-quantity invariant before creating an `OrderLine`. The order can later add duplicate-product rules, recalculate totals, or publish an event without hunting for arbitrary list mutations throughout the codebase. The C# example returns an array snapshot, so callers do not see later changes through an allegedly read-only view. `AsReadOnly` would prevent mutation through that reference but would still expose live changes; either choice can be valid when documented. Encapsulate Collection is about ownership of mutation, not automatically copying every list. For large collections, exposing an iterator or purpose-specific query may avoid repeated snapshots.
concepts.caution: A read-only interface can still be a live view over mutable storage. Decide whether callers need a stable snapshot, and account for the copying cost.
concepts.related: Encapsulate Field is the scalar counterpart. Aggregate roots commonly use this technique to protect child-entity invariants.

concepts.title: Replace Type Code with Class
concepts.definition: Replace a primitive category code with a named value type that owns the valid set and domain vocabulary.
concepts.look_for: Strings or integers representing a category are passed widely, compared repeatedly, or confused with unrelated primitives.
concepts.python_shorthand:
from enum import Enum


class ShippingServiceLevel(Enum):
    STANDARD = "STANDARD"
    EXPRESS = "EXPRESS"


shipment = Shipment(ShippingServiceLevel.EXPRESS)
concepts.walkthrough: A raw string such as `"EXPRESS"` accepts misspellings and can be confused with any other string. `ShippingServiceLevel` makes the category a named domain type. The C# constructor is private, so clients must choose one of the canonical `Standard` or `Express` instances; equality compares codes rather than references. The expanded Python class validates the code and defines the same value semantics, while the `Enum` shorthand is the usual choice for a small closed set. `Shipment` now advertises that it requires a shipping service level rather than arbitrary text. This refactoring centralizes valid values and vocabulary but does not yet move substantially different shipping algorithms into the type. If conditionals based on the code spread across the system, Replace Type Code with Subclasses or State/Strategy may be the next step. If the set comes from a database and changes at runtime, a closed enum may be too rigid.
concepts.caution: Do not model externally configurable categories as a compile-time closed set without considering versioning and unknown values.
concepts.related: Use subclasses when categories have stable distinct behavior; use State or Strategy when behavior changes or is selected independently.

concepts.title: Replace Type Code with Subclasses
concepts.definition: Replace a stable type code and repeated branches with subclasses that implement the behavior for each enduring subtype.
concepts.look_for: The same type-code switch appears in several operations, each instance keeps one type for life, and every subtype is substitutable through a common contract.
concepts.walkthrough: Instead of storing `TypeCode` and switching inside `CalculatePay`, the refactored model creates a `SalariedEmployee` or `HourlyEmployee`. Each subclass implements `CalculateWeeklyPay`/`calculate_weekly_pay` with the state relevant to that employment type. Payroll code can hold an `Employee` and invoke one common operation without knowing the concrete subtype. Adding another operation that varies by employment type places its implementation beside the same subtype, eliminating another repeated switch. The important precondition is stable identity: an employee should not need to change concrete runtime type every week. If compensation policy can be swapped independently or combined with other dimensions, a `PayStrategy` collaborator is more flexible. A single small closed switch may also be clearer than a hierarchy. The refactoring earns the subclass structure only when behavior clusters by a durable, substitutable category.
concepts.caution: Do not build a hierarchy for a tiny closed switch or a category that changes at runtime. Inheritance commits the model to a stable taxonomy.
concepts.related: Replace Conditional with Polymorphism describes the behavioral result. Strategy is preferable when the varying policy is replaceable or combinable.

concepts.title: Replace Type Code with State/Strategy
concepts.definition: Replace a code-driven branch with an object that owns the selected behavior, using State for lifecycle-driven changes or Strategy for caller-selected policy.
concepts.look_for: A context repeatedly switches on a status or mode, and the corresponding behavior needs to evolve, be tested independently, or change without replacing the context.
concepts.walkthrough: The earlier form would typically store a service-level code and branch inside `ShippingQuote.Calculate`. Here, `ShippingQuote` keeps only the stable workflow: ask its `_rateStrategy` to calculate the rate for a parcel. `StandardShippingRate` and `ExpressShippingRate` own the formulas that used to occupy separate switch branches, and the caller selects one when constructing the quote. This instance is Strategy because policy choice comes from outside the context. The same object-oriented move becomes State when the context changes the collaborator as part of its lifecycle and each state governs permitted transitions. In both cases, behavior replaces a code that merely selected behavior. The interface makes each alternative independently testable and lets new rate policies arrive without editing `ShippingQuote`. The cost is extra types and indirection; a dictionary or switch remains sensible for a small, closed set with trivial behavior.
concepts.caution: Do not confuse Strategy with State: callers select a strategy, while state transitions usually belong to the context's lifecycle. Use objects only when behavior justifies them.
concepts.related: Strategy and State share a shape but differ in intent. Replace Type Code with Subclasses fits stable intrinsic categories rather than replaceable policy.

concepts.title: Replace Subclass with Fields
concepts.definition: Replace subclasses that differ only by constant data with one class whose fields represent that variation.
concepts.look_for: Subclasses contain no distinct algorithms or invariants; they only override methods to return different names, rates, or flags.
concepts.walkthrough: `BasicTier` and `PremiumTier` previously existed only to override a name and discount constant. The refactored `CustomerTier` stores those differences in `Name`/`name` and `DiscountRate`/`discount_rate`, while `DiscountFor`/`discount_for` holds the one shared calculation. `Basic` and `Premium` are now configured instances rather than empty subclasses. Clients still ask a tier for its discount, but adding another purely data-defined tier no longer requires another class. This is the right simplification when subclass identity carries no special invariant or behavior. It is not an argument to replace all polymorphism with flags: if premium pricing later gains a cap, loyalty threshold, or different calculation, separate strategies may again become honest. The refactoring removes a taxonomy that encoded data as types and leaves variation in the place it actually exists.
concepts.caution: Keep subclasses when they protect different invariants or own genuinely different behavior. Fields are appropriate only for data-shaped variation.
concepts.related: This is the reverse pressure of Replace Type Code with Subclasses. Data-driven instances can also be Flyweights when shared widely.

chapters.title: Simplifying conditional expressions
chapters.intro: These refactorings turn control flow into named decisions and make the happy path easy to see.

concepts.title: Decompose Conditional
concepts.definition: Extract a complicated condition and its branches into named operations that state the business decision.
concepts.look_for: A conditional mixes dates, calculations, and several boolean clauses, forcing readers to decode mechanics before understanding the rule.
concepts.walkthrough: The before form makes the reader translate `DueDate < today && !IsPaid` into the domain idea overdue, then separately infer what each branch means. The after form names all three ideas: `IsOverdue`, `ApplyLateFee`, and `HandleCurrentInvoice`, with Python equivalents. The condition still evaluates the same fields, the late fee is still two percent of the balance, and the same reminder method runs on the other path. Only the organization changes. This refactoring is useful because names become stable landmarks even when the mechanical rule grows. It also creates focused places for tests or later policy changes. Extraction is not automatically clearer: a two-clause condition whose meaning is already obvious may be easier to read inline, especially if the new methods are far away. The goal is to expose the business decision, not maximize the method count.
concepts.caution: Do not fragment a tiny obvious branch into distant methods. Extraction should reduce interpretation, not force navigation.
concepts.related: Consolidate Conditional Expression names one shared reason across several checks. Replace Conditional with Polymorphism addresses repeated variation across types.

concepts.title: Consolidate Conditional Expression
concepts.definition: Combine checks that lead to the same outcome when they express one higher-level business reason.
concepts.look_for: Several adjacent conditions return or branch identically, and callers would understand them better as one named predicate.
concepts.walkthrough: All three before checks return zero pay. `IsIneligibleForPay`/`is_ineligible_for_pay` reveals that they are not three arbitrary early exits; together they define one eligibility rule. The order of pure boolean checks does not affect the result here, and short-circuit evaluation remains in place. A caller can now read the high-level decision in one phrase, while the predicate contains the exact policy. This consolidation is safe only because termination, unpaid leave, and starting after the period genuinely belong to the same concept and share the same outcome. If termination later requires a final-payment calculation while unpaid leave remains zero, they should separate again. Conditions with side effects, exception-prone calls, or deliberately ordered diagnostics also require care because combining them can change which operations execute.
concepts.caution: Combine conditions by meaning, not merely because they happen to return the same value today. Preserve evaluation order when checks have effects or can fail.
concepts.related: Decompose Conditional extracts names for branches. Guard Clauses flatten exceptional paths but need not combine their reasons.

concepts.title: Consolidate Duplicate Conditional Fragments
concepts.definition: Move identical work out of every branch so the conditional contains only the behavior that actually varies.
concepts.look_for: Each branch begins or ends with the same statement, obscuring the one branch-specific operation.
concepts.walkthrough: Both original branches end with `audit.Write(order.Id)` or `audit.write(order.id)`. Moving that call after the conditional leaves only `MarkPaid` versus `MarkPaymentFailed` inside the branches, so the true variation is immediately visible. For normal completion, observable behavior is unchanged: the order changes state and then one audit record is written. Exception order matters, however. The extracted audit call still does not run if either state-change method throws, matching the before form. Moving a shared statement from the beginning of branches to before the conditional, or across a call that may throw, deserves the same analysis. Duplicate fragments sometimes signal a larger operation that should be extracted, but the small movement alone can clarify the branch without inventing another abstraction.
concepts.caution: Verify side-effect and exception order. Textually identical statements are not safely movable across every operation.
concepts.related: Slide Statements is the more general movement refactoring. Decompose Conditional can then name the remaining branch-specific work.

concepts.title: Remove Control Flag
concepts.definition: Replace a boolean used to simulate loop exit or return with direct control flow.
concepts.look_for: Readers must track a flag across several paths to determine whether a loop continues or a result has already been found.
concepts.walkthrough: `found` does not represent durable domain state; it exists solely to prevent the loop from doing more work after finding an overdue order. The after form states that control decision directly with `return`. The method still returns the first overdue order, or null/`None` when no match exists, but readers no longer simulate a boolean across later iterations. `break` would be appropriate if cleanup or result construction had to occur after the loop. A collection query may offer further shorthand, but the explicit loop shows the semantic change most clearly. Control flags are legitimate in state machines, parsers, and algorithms where the flag names an actual state that affects future transitions. The smell is a mutable boolean that merely imitates a language control construct.
concepts.caution: Do not erase meaningful algorithmic state. Remove flags only when `return`, `break`, or `continue` states the same control decision more directly.
concepts.related: Replace Loop with Pipeline can express this search as `FirstOrDefault` or `next`, but direct control flow is often the clearest intermediate step.

concepts.title: Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses
concepts.definition: Handle invalid, exceptional, or terminating cases early so the normal path is not buried in nested blocks.
concepts.look_for: The main operation sits several indentation levels deep because each preceding condition wraps the remainder of the method.
concepts.walkthrough: The nested version expresses the ordinary pay calculation only after proving two negative conditions. The refactored method handles termination and unpaid leave first, then leaves `CalculateRegularPay`/`calculate_regular_pay` as the unindented main path. Each case returns the same value as before; only the order in which the reader encounters the cases changes. Guard clauses work well when the handled cases terminate the method and do not share a long teardown sequence. They also make precondition failures visible near the top of a function. Multiple early exits can be harmful when a lifecycle requires one obvious cleanup point or when dozens of validation rules obscure the operation. In those cases, a named validator, result type, or `try/finally` boundary can preserve structure better than an unbounded list of guards.
concepts.caution: Keep cleanup and transactional boundaries obvious. Many guards that form one coherent validation policy should usually be grouped behind a named operation.
concepts.related: Consolidate Conditional Expression can combine guards with one meaning. Assertions are for programmer invariants, not ordinary guard validation.

concepts.title: Replace Conditional with Polymorphism
concepts.definition: Move each branch of repeated type-based logic into the object or strategy responsible for that behavior.
concepts.look_for: The same switch over type, status, or mode appears in several operations, and adding one alternative requires editing each switch.
concepts.walkthrough: A switch in `Checkout` would make it responsible for every shipping formula. After the refactoring, `GroundShipping.CalculateCost` and `AirShipping.CalculateCost` own their respective branches, while `Checkout.ShippingCost` makes one polymorphic call through `IShippingMethod`/`ShippingMethod`. Adding a new shipping method can leave checkout unchanged, and tests can exercise each formula directly. The refactoring is valuable when the same alternatives drive several behaviors or are expected to expand. It is not inherently superior to a switch. A modern pattern match over a small, closed set keeps all cases visible and may be easier to audit. The example has the shape of Strategy because the caller supplies the shipping method; subclass polymorphism and Strategy are implementation and design labels that can overlap. The central improvement is relocating behavior to the owner of the variation, not merely replacing `switch` with virtual dispatch.
concepts.caution: A hierarchy or strategy family adds navigation and types. Keep a clear switch when the alternatives are small, closed, and naturally reviewed together.
concepts.related: Closely related to Replace Type Code with State/Strategy and Strategy. Pattern matching is a modern alternative for closed algebraic cases.

concepts.title: Introduce Null Object
concepts.definition: Represent ordinary absence with an object that provides stable neutral behavior, removing repeated null checks from clients.
concepts.look_for: Many callers perform the same null check and choose the same harmless fallback behavior.
concepts.walkthrough: `OrderService` always holds an object implementing `IAuditLog` or the expected Python protocol. When no real audit sink is configured, the constructor substitutes `NullAuditLog`, whose `Write`/`write` method deliberately has no effect. `Cancel` can therefore perform one unconditional collaboration instead of repeating `if (_auditLog != null)` in every operation. Absence is safe here because audit output is explicitly optional in this teaching scenario. This is a Null Object; Fowler's newer term Introduce Special Case is broader and can represent behavior for anonymous customers, unknown values, or other distinguished cases. The pattern becomes dangerous when the missing collaborator is required for correctness, compliance, or security. A no-op audit logger in a regulated production path could silently violate requirements. In those cases construction should fail or the operation should return an explicit error.
concepts.caution: Neutral behavior must be genuinely safe. Never let a null object hide missing required data, authorization, persistence, or compliance work.
concepts.related: Introduce Special Case generalizes this refactoring. Option/Maybe and Result types preserve absence explicitly instead of replacing it with behavior.

concepts.title: Introduce Assertion
concepts.definition: Encode an invariant that correct program logic should already guarantee, so violations fail near their cause and document the assumption.
concepts.look_for: Later code relies on a condition that is guaranteed only implicitly by earlier internal operations.
concepts.walkthrough: `ShipPaidOrder`/`_ship_paid_order` is an internal step whose callers are supposed to establish `Paid` status first. The assertion records that invariant at the point where shipping relies on it. If an internal control-flow bug sends a draft order here during development or testing, failure occurs beside the broken assumption rather than after an invalid shipment. The assertion is not input validation: a user submitting an unpaid order is an expected external condition and must receive a normal validation result or exception that remains active in production. C# `Debug.Assert` may not stop release execution, and Python assertions disappear under optimized execution. That is acceptable only because correct production behavior does not depend on the assertion. Assertions serve as executable documentation and diagnostic tripwires; they do not replace domain guards, security checks, or recoverable error handling.
concepts.caution: Assume assertions may be disabled. Validate untrusted input and enforce business or security rules with ordinary production code.
concepts.related: Guard Clauses handle expected invalid cases. Design by Contract distinguishes preconditions, postconditions, and invariants more formally.
